content: Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) has been increasingly utilized as a treatment option for atopic eczema. A prior Cochrane review from 2004 suggested a potential benefit of oral CHM for eczema, but the evidence was inconclusive and required further investigation. This updated review expanded its scope to evaluate both oral and topical applications of CHM for eczema management in children and adults. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was performed up to September 2012, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, LILACS, CINAHL, SCOPUS, HERBMED, ProQuest, CQVIP, CNKI, and Wanfang Data. Additional sources such as trial registries, conference proceedings, reference lists, and expert consultations were also utilized. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CHM to placebo, no intervention, active controls (e.g., acupuncture), or conventional medicines. A total of 28 studies involving 2306 participants were included in the analysis. Most studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias, particularly in terms of blinding of participants and personnel. This inconsistency across studies necessitates caution when interpreting any positive effects of CHM. Notably, four studies from the previous review were excluded because they investigated a CHM product that had been withdrawn from the market since 2004. Four studies (three oral and one topical) compared CHM to placebo. Pooled data from two studies demonstrated that the total effectiveness rate in the CHM group was higher (risk ratio [RR] 2.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.32 to 3.32; 2 studies; n = 85). Additionally, the itching visual analogue score (VAS) was 1.53 points lower in the CHM group (standardized mean difference [SMD], 95% CI -2.64 to -0.41; 2 studies; n = 94), indicating reduced itch severity. One study involving 85 participants with moderate to severe eczema reported a quality of life (QoL) score that was 2.5 points lower in the CHM group (mean difference [MD], 95% CI -4.77 to -0.23; 1 study; n = 85), where a lower score reflects better QoL. Twenty-two studies and one arm of a four-arm parallel controlled study compared CHM (5 oral, 6 topical, and 12 mixed oral and topical) to conventional medicines. The total effectiveness rate in the CHM groups was higher (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.27 to 1.61; 21 studies; n = 1868; very low-quality evidence). The itching VAS was also 0.83 points lower in the CHM groups (SMD, 95% CI -1.43 to -0.22; 7 studies; n = 465) compared to conventional treatments. Two studies compared combined oral and topical CHM to oral CHM alone. In one study, the total effectiveness rate was not statistically significant (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.63; 1 study; n = 20). In the other study, the itching VAS was 1.05 points lower in the combined CHM group (MD, 95% CI -1.75 to -0.35; 1 study; n = 23). Regarding adverse events, four studies did not report any side effects. The remaining 24 studies documented minor adverse events, which resolved shortly after discontinuing CHM. However, one participant withdrew from a trial due to worsening of their condition following CHM use. Eight studies received government funding. In conclusion, this review did not find conclusive evidence that CHM, whether taken orally or applied topically, significantly reduces the severity of eczema in children or adults. Further well-designed, adequately powered RCTs are necessary to determine the efficacy and safety of CHM for eczema management.
